candidate_relations.reason: Biopsy shows a clean split above the stratum granulosum and complete stratum-corneum separation rather than the retained or abnormal cornification pattern of ichthyosis.
Early-onset frictional superficial peeling, a subcorneal split, and two CDSN exon-2 variants identify the same CDSN-related peeling skin syndrome.
Mild xerosis accompanies the erosions but cannot explain the sharply superficial peeling plane or the pathogenic CDSN findings.
There was no blistering and immunofluorescence mapping of collagen IV/VII, integrins, and laminin-332 was normal, opposing epidermolysis bullosa.
Celiac serologies were negative and there are no gastrointestinal or malabsorptive findings linking the skin fragility to celiac disease.
Keratolysis exfoliativa is usually limited to palms and soles, whereas this child has inherited early-infantile peeling across friction sites including the trunk and has CDSN variants.
The dominant lesion is effortless superficial erosion from stratum-corneum detachment, not persistent generalized hyperkeratotic scale typical of inherited ichthyosis.
Keratolytic winter erythema worsens in winter and is palmoplantar, while this child's disease improves in winter, worsens in summer, and affects trunk friction areas.
CDSN variants can cause type-B peeling skin syndrome, but the record does not explicitly establish the inflammatory subtype and describes only mild xerosis without a clear atopic phenotype.
Normal hair and the absence of atopy or ichthyosis linearis circumflexa do not support Netherton syndrome, and testing instead found CDSN variants.
The child has no blisters and normal basement-membrane immunofluorescence mapping, whereas histology places the split above the granular layer.
There was no collodion membrane or generalized plate-like scale, and the biopsy-genetic combination supports peeling skin disease rather than autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis.
The label matches the diagnosis established by effortless superficial peeling, a split just above the granular layer, and biallelic-appearing heterozygous CDSN exon-2 variants.
Erosions occur across the trunk and multiple friction sites rather than a single acral area, fitting generalized peeling skin syndrome within the referenced peeling skin disease.
Summer worsening and winter improvement describe a trigger pattern, but do not account for the histologic stratum-corneum split or CDSN mutations.
A CDSN-related superficial peeling disorder is the same disease demonstrated by supragranular separation and early-onset skin fragility in this child.
This candidate directly names peeling skin disease due to the CDSN mutations found in exon 2 and matches the characteristic superficial cleavage plane.
Two CDSN variants make a genetic disorder plausible, but this phrase loses the specific skin-peeling phenotype and molecular diagnosis.
Peeling skin disease exactly matches the reference and is supported by painless superficial stripping with a clean split above the granular layer.
The child has superficial erosions involving the trunk and friction sites without focal acral hyperkeratotic papules.
